items.title: battledrones v14: Compass Rose, a four player map
items.description: Release: battledrones v14: Compass Rose, a four player map I added four player online mode to Battledrones - previous maps were limited to two. Here's the initial prompt I used: Add a new map for a four player battle - four way rotational symmetry, up to four AI players, works with the WebSocket non-audio based multiplayer mode so up to four human players can join (any spare slots use AI) Claude Opus 4.5 added a new map called "Compass Rose" and modified the WebSockets multiplayer network code to support up to four players for that map, joining via share links or QR codes. The new teams use robots themed in purple and green, joining the existing blue and red designs. You can preview those colors in the updated model browser . Here's a replay link to watch a four way AI battle with the "Goliath Armada" mutator turned on, where each side starts with four giant Goliath mech units. Tags: game-design , projects , claude

items.title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
items.description: Using Google's products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world's largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won't use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company's privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall. On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy , spotted by Android Authority . The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. "We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos," the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language. Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads. Credit: Google This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it's shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026 , allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it's also proving to be a privacy minefield. Read full article Comments

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.description: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. items.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
items.description: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier. Supported models and AWS Regions MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter: Base model AWS Regions Amazon Nova 2 Lite US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) GPT-OSS-20B US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned) US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Qwen 3.6 27B US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list. Pricing You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model: Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history. Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens. Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter. The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339: Dimension Tokens Price per 1M Cost Prefill 491,616,806 $0.12 $58.99 Sample 159,737,098 $0.30 $47.92 Train 643,308,554 $0.36 $231.59 Total 1,294,662,458 $338.50 The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under Billa

items.title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
items.description: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/ /variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update. Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an on_event handler that returns immediately and an is_complete handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation. A ConfigHash property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single ConfigHash drives the auto scaling orchestration. While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK cr.Provider , and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three ( onEvent , isComplete , and onTimeout ) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an on_event and is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources. Walkthrough In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly. items.description: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field , which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer. Example: LineString layer Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [-73.7781, 40.6413], [-85.5627, 40.6407], [-97.1415, 39.4569], [-108.1612, 37.1753], [-118.4085, 33.9416] ] }, "properties": { "route_id": "JFK-LAX" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 1: Dataset row for the JFK-LAX route, keyed by route_id The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines. Figure 2: The JFK-LAX route drawn as a LineString layer Example: Point layer Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [-73.9490, 40.7447] }, "properties": { "store_id": "S-109" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 3: Dataset row for a store, keyed by store_id The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points. Figure 4: A store plotted as a Point layer Lines on layer map visuals Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence. Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as fli

items.title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
items.description: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code. Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge. When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes. items.title: AIコーディングエージェントとは？主要10ツール比較と無料で始める選び方
items.description: AIコーディングエージェントとは、指示を受けて計画からコード編集、テスト、PR作成まで自律的に進める開発AIです。本記事では、 2026年10月時点の主要10ツールを5つの軸で比較 し、目的別の選び方と始め方を解説します。 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Devinなど、AIコーディングエージェントは毎月のように新機能の追加や改名が続いています。どれが自分やチームに合うのか判断できず、試す前に迷っている方も多いでしょう。 ツール選びの近道は、動作環境・無料枠・日本語対応などの軸を先に決めて比べることです。IDC Japanの調査では、AIが主体でコードを生成している国内企業は11.4%で、3年後には35.1%に増える見通しです。 出典： 国内AIコード生成、3年後に3倍超へ（IDC Japan） 古い情報のままツールを選ぶと、契約や設定のやり直しが発生します。反対に、自分に合う1つを見極めて小さなタスクから任せれば、実装を任せた分の時間を設計やレビューに回せます。 本記事では、補完型AIとの違いと、 無料枠と日本語対応まで含めた主要10ツールの比較表 を中心に解説します。読み終えるころには、自分に合うツールを1つ選び、無料枠で試し始められる状態になるでしょう。ぜひ最後まで読み進めてください。 AIコーディングエージェントとは自律的に開発を進めるAI AIコーディングエージェントは、 「この機能を追加して」というタスク単位の指示で動く開発AI です。理解するためのポイントは以下の3つです。 コード補完型AIとの違い ChatGPTなどチャット型AIとの違い AIコーディングエージェントが動く仕組み 違いと仕組みを押さえておくと、ツールを比べるときに「どこまで任せられるか」で判断できます。 コード補完型AIとの違い コード補完型AIとAIコーディングエージェントの違いは、 作業を進める主体が人かAIか という点にあります。 補完型AIは、人が書いているコードの続きを数行単位で提案する道具です。主導権は人にあり、AIは入力速度を上げる役割にとどまります。 比較項目 コード補完型AI AIコーディングエージェント 作業の単位 カーソル周辺の数行 機能追加やバグ修正などのタスク1つ 作業を進める主体 人が書き、AIが候補を出す AIが計画して進め、人が確認する 扱える範囲 開いているファイルが中心 リポジトリ全体、ターミナル、Git 人の役割 候補を採用するか選ぶ タスクを定義し、成果物をレビューする たとえばGitHub Copilotのインライン補完は補完型、Copilotのエージェントモードはエージェント型に分類できます。同じツール名でも機能ごとに型が異なる点に注意が必要です。 補完型に慣れている方ほど、エージェント型では 「書く人」から「任せて確認する人」 へ役割が移ると捉えると、使い方のイメージがつかみやすくなります。 ChatGPTなどチャット型AIとの違い チャット型AIとの違いは、 コードを書いた後の実行と修正まで自分で進めるかどうか です。 ChatGPTやClaudeのチャット画面にコードを頼むと、回答としてコードが返ってきます。ただし、そのコードを貼り付けて動かし、エラーを直すのは人の作業です。 AIコーディングエージェントは、手元のファイルを直接編集し、テストやビルドのコマンドも実行します。エラーが出れば原因を調べて修正し、通るまで同じ流れを繰り返します。 コピー＆ペーストの往復がなくなるため、複数ファイルにまたがる修正ほど差が大きくなります。チャット型で「コードは出るが動かすまでが面倒」と感じていた方は、エージェント型で手間を減らせるでしょう。 AIコーディングエージェントが動く仕組み AIコーディングエージェントは、 「考える→ツールを使う→結果を読む」というループ を繰り返して作業を進めます。流れは以下のとおりです。 指示とコードベースを読み、作業計画を立てる ファイルの編集やコマンドの実行など、ツールを呼び出す テスト結果やエラーを読み、次の手を決める 完了条件を満たすまで1〜3を繰り返す 頭脳にあたるのはLLM（大規模言語モデル）で、手足にあたるのがファイル操作やターミナルなどのツールです。プロジェクトの規約やテスト方法は、AGENTS.mdなどの設定ファイルから読み込みます。 仕組みを知っておくと、エージェントが迷ったときに「計画」「ツール」「設定ファイル」のどこを直せばよいか判断できます。 AIコーディングエージェントは動く場所で3種類に分かれる AIコーディングエージェントは、 動く場所によって以下の3種類 に分かれます。 IDE型：エディタで一手ずつ確認しながら進める CLI型：ターミナルで要所だけ承認して任せる クラウド型：非同期で任せてPRで受け取る 種類によって人が関わるタイミングが変わるため、自分の働き方に合う型から選ぶと失敗しにくくなります。 【IDE型】エディタで一手ずつ確認しながら進める IDE型は、VS Codeなどのエディタの中で動くタイプです。 変更内容を画面上の差分で1つずつ確認しながら進められる 点が特徴です。 エージェントがファイルを書き換えるたびに、追加行と削除行が色分けで表示されます。気になる変更はその場で却下できるため、AIに任せる範囲を細かく調整できます。 代表例は、GitHub Copilotのエージェントモード、Cursor、Cline、Kiroです。普段の開発環境を大きく変えずに導入できます。 エージェントにまだ不安がある方でも、慣れた画面で挙動を観察しながら任せる範囲を広げていけます。 【CLI型】ターミナルで要所だけ承認して任せる CLI型は、ターミナル上で対話しながら動くタイプです。 ファイル編集やコマンド実行など、要所だけ人が承認して任せる 使い方に向いています。 エディタに依存しないため、VS Code派でもJetBrains派でも同じように使えます。Gitやテストのコマンドと組み合わせやすく、大きな改修を一気に進める場面で力を発揮します。 代表例は、Claude Code、Codex CLI、Antigravity CLI、Aiderです。どのツールも、承認なしで実行してよい操作の範囲を設定で変えられます。 ターミナル操作に慣れたエンジニアなら、エディタを切り替えずに開発の流れへ組み込めるでしょう。 【クラウド型】非同期で任せてPRで受け取る クラウド型は、ベンダーが用意した仮想環境でエージェントが動くタイプです。 タスクを渡したら手を離し、完成したPR（プルリクエスト）をレビューする 流れになります。 手元のPCを占有しないため、複数のタスクを並行して任せられます。たとえばGitHub Copilotのcloud agentは、Issueを割り当てるとクラウド上で実装とテストを行い、PRを作成します。 出典： GitHub Copilot cloud agentについて（GitHub Docs） 代表例は、Copilot cloud agent、Codexのクラウド版、Jules、Devinです。人が関わるのは最初の指示と最後のレビューが中心です。 会議や別作業の間に定型的な修正を片付けておけるため、チーム全体の処理量を底上げしたい場面に向いています。 AIコーディングエージェントを比較する5つの軸 AIコーディングエージェントを比較するときは、 以下の5つの軸 で見ると違いが整理できます。 動作環境 無料枠と料金体系 自律性と承認の細かさ 日本語指示への対応 セキュリティと権限管理 ベンチマークの順位だけで選ぶと、自分の環境で使いにくいツールを契約してしまうため注意しましょう。 動作環境 最初に確認したいのは、 普段の開発環境で無理なく使えるか です。IDE型・CLI型・クラウド型のどれに当たるかで、導入の手間が変わります。 たとえばCursorは独自のエディタなので、VS Codeから乗り換える必要があります。一方でClineはVS CodeとJetBrainsの拡張機能として動くため、今のエディタに追加するだけで使えます。 クラウド型の場合は、GitHubなど使っているリポジトリサービスと連携できるかも重要です。JulesやCopilot cloud agentはGitHubとの連携が前提になっています。 動作環境が合えば、導入初日から実務のタスクで試せるため、効果を判断するまでの時間を短くできます。 無料枠と料金体系 料金は月額の安さだけでなく、 無料枠の有無と課金の単位 まで確認しましょう。 課金の方式は、大きく以下の3つに分かれます。 月額サブスク型：Claude Code、Copilot、Cursorなど。プランごとに利用上限がある クレジット型：Kiroなど。月ごとに付与されるクレジットを消費する BYOK型：Cline、Aiderなど。ツールは無料で、使ったAIのAPI料金だけを払う BYOK（Bring Your Own Key）は、自分で契約したAPIキーを持ち込む方式です。使った分だけ支払うため、使用量が少ない月は安く済みます。 ただし、大きなタスクを任せるとAPI料金が想定より膨らむことがあります。 無料枠で使用量の感覚をつかんでから 有料プランを選ぶと、無駄な出費を防げます。 自律性と承認の細かさ ツールによって、 人の承認なしにどこまで進めるか が異なります。任せたい仕事の大きさに合わせて選ぶことが大切です。 Clineはファイル編集やコマンド実行のたびに承認を求める設計です。一方、Devinやクラウド型のツールは、指示を受けたらPR作成まで自律的に進めます。 自律性が高いほど人の手間は減りますが、意図しない変更に気づくのが遅れます。初めて使う場合は承認を細かく挟めるツールで挙動を確かめ、慣れてから任せる範囲を広げるのが安全です。 承認の細かさを自分で調整できるツールを選んでおけば、チームの習熟度に合わせて運用を変えていけます。 日本語指示への対応 日本語で指示を出したい方は、 公式に日本語対応を明記しているか を確認しましょう。多くのツールは日本語でも動きますが、公式の対応状況には差があります。 Kiroはチャットの対応言語に日本語を明記しています。Devinはリリースノートで日本語での応答と画面の日本語化に対応したと案内しています。 一方で、GitHub Copilot Chatは主な対応言語を英語としており、PRの要約やコミットメッセージの生成は英語のみです。Julesは「現時点では英語でのみ利用可能」と案内されています。 出典： Responsible use of GitHub Copilot Chat（GitHub Docs） 英語が主のツールでも日本語の指示は通りますが、精度が落ちることがあります。日本語で仕様を書くチームは、対応言語を事前に確認しておくと手戻りを防げます。 セキュリティと権限管理 業務で使う場合は、 ソースコードの扱いと、エージェントに与える権限の範囲 を確認する必要があります。 確認したいポイントは以下の3つです。 入力したコードがAIの学習に使われない設定にできるか 書き込みやコマンド実行の範囲を制限できるか 操作のログを残し、後から確認できるか ソースコードを社外に出せない場合は、ローカルLLM（自分のPCで動かすAIモデル）に対応したツールが候補になります。Cline、Aiderはどちらもローカルモデルで動かせます。 セキュリティ要件を先に固めておくと、情報システム部門の審査で差し戻されることなく導入を進められます。 おすすめのAIコーディングエージェント10選を比較 2026年10月時点で おすすめのAIコーディングエージェントは以下の10個 です。 ツール 提供元 動作環境 無料枠 個人向け最安の有料プラン Claude Code Anthropic CLI型・IDE拡張・Web なし Pro：$20/月 OpenAI Codex OpenAI CLI型・IDE拡張・クラウド型 あり Go：$8/月 GitHub Copilot GitHub IDE型・クラウド型 あり Pro：$10/月 Cursor Anysphere エディタ一体型 あり Plus：$8/月 Devin Cognition クラウド型・エディタ一体型 あり Pro：$20/月 Kiro AWS IDE型・CLI型 あり Pro：$20/月 Jules Google クラウド型 あり Google AIの有料プランで枠が拡大 Google Antigravity Google IDE型・CLI型・アプリ あり Google AIの有料プランで枠が拡大 Cline Cline Bot IDE型・CLI型 あり なし（API料金のみ） Aider オープンソース CLI型 あり なし（API料金のみ） ※料金は2026年10月23日時点の各社公式サイトの米ドル表記（税抜）です。 料金やプランは変更が多いため、契約前に各公式サイトで最新情報を確認してください。 Claude Code：大規模な改修までターミナルで任せられる Claude Codeは、Anthropicが提供するCLI型のエージェントです。 コードベース全体を読み込んだうえで、複数ファイルにまたがる改修を任せられる 点が強みです。 items.title: AIエージェントの仕組みとは？4つの構成要素と動く流れをわかりやすく解説
items.description: 「AIエージェントは自律的に動く」と聞いても、内部で何が起きているのかを説明できず困っていないでしょうか。 AIエージェントの仕組みは、 LLMが頭脳となり、ツールとメモリを使って「考える・行動する・確かめる」を繰り返す構造 です。 仕組みを知らないまま導入すると、任せる範囲や権限を誤り、誤操作や情報漏えいを招きます。反対に仕組みを理解していれば、ベンダーの提案が妥当かを自分で見極められます。 本記事では、AIエージェントを構成する4つの要素と、業務の具体例で追う動作の流れを中心に解説します。 読み終える頃には、AIエージェントの仕組みを社内で説明でき、どの業務を任せるべきかを判断できるようになります。 AIエージェントの仕組みはLLMを中心にした制御ループ AIエージェントは、LLMが次の行動を決め、ツールで実行し、結果を見て再び判断する 制御ループ で動きます。まずは全体像と、各社の解説に共通する構造を確認しましょう。 AIエージェントは目標から手順を自分で組み立てる AIエージェントは、人が手順を細かく指示しなくても、 目標を渡すだけで作業の手順を自分で組み立てます 。 中心にいるLLMが、目標と現在の状況を読み取り、次に何をすべきかを毎回判断しているためです。判断した行動はツールで実行され、その結果が再びLLMに渡されます。 たとえば「来週の会議資料を準備して」と頼むと、関連ファイルの検索、要点の整理、資料の作成という順番をAIエージェント自身が決めます。ファイルが見つからなければ、別の場所を探す軌道修正も行います。 Anthropicも、エージェントを「LLMが自らの処理の流れとツールの使い方を動的に決めるシステム」と定義しています。 出典： 『Building effective agents』（Anthropic） 手順ではなく目標で指示できる点を押さえると、 AIエージェントに任せる業務の切り出し方 が見えてきます。 主要各社の解説も同じ構造に行き着く AIエージェントの構成要素は解説によって呼び方が異なりますが、 中身はほぼ同じ部品に整理できます 。 どの解説も「判断する部品」「振る舞いを決める部品」「外部に働きかける部品」「記憶する部品」を、別の言葉で説明しているためです。 出典 判断する部品 振る舞いを決める部品 外部に働きかける部品 記憶する部品 Anthropic LLM 記載なし ツール・検索 メモリ OpenAI Agents SDK モデル 指示 ツール 基本設定には含まれない Wangらのサーベイ論文 計画 プロファイル 行動 メモリ 出典： 『Building effective agents』（Anthropic） 出典： 『Agents』（OpenAI Agents SDK） 出典： 『A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents』（arXiv） 本記事では、この共通部分を 「LLM・指示・ツール・メモリ」の4要素 として解説します。名称が違う資料を読むときも、どの部品の話かを対応づけられるようになります。 AIエージェントを構成する4つの要素 AIエージェントは、以下の4つの要素の組み合わせで動いています。 LLM：状況を読み取り次の行動を決める頭脳 指示：役割とルールを定める設計図 ツール：検索やシステム操作を担う手足 メモリ：経緯と知識を保持する記憶 どれか1つが欠けても、AIエージェントは目標どおりに動けません。 LLM：状況を読み取り次の行動を決める頭脳 LLM（大規模言語モデル）は、AIエージェントの中で 次に何をするかを決める判断役 です。 LLMは文章を理解し生成する能力を持つため、目標・指示・これまでの結果をまとめて読み取り、次の一手を出力できます。OpenAIのGPTシリーズ、AnthropicのClaude、GoogleのGeminiが代表例です。 ただし、LLM自体は文章を出力するだけで、メール送信やファイル保存などの操作は行えません。操作は後述のツールが担い、LLMは「どのツールを、どの値で使うか」を指示します。 判断の質はLLMの性能に左右されます。ベンダーの提案を比較するときは、 どのLLMを採用しているか を確認すると違いを把握しやすくなります。 指示：役割とルールを定める設計図 指示は、AIエージェントの 役割・守るべきルール・完了の条件 を定める設定です。システムプロンプトとも呼ばれます。 同じLLMでも、指示が曖昧だと判断がぶれ、不要な操作をしたり途中で止まったりします。OpenAIのAgents SDKでも、指示の設定は「強く推奨」とされています。 出典： 『Agents』（OpenAI Agents SDK） 指示には、以下のような内容を書きます。 役割：「あなたは経理部の請求書処理担当です」 ルール：「10万円を超える支払いは処理せず、担当者に確認する」 完了条件：「全件を会計システムに登録したら終了する」 現場のルールを指示に落とし込むほど判断が安定します。AIエージェントの品質は、 業務を知る担当者がどれだけ関わるか で大きく変わります。 ツール：検索やシステム操作を担う手足 ツールは、AIエージェントが 外部の情報を取りに行ったり、システムを操作したりするための機能 です。 LLMは学習時点までの知識しか持たず、外部のシステムにも直接触れられません。ツールを持たせることで、最新情報の検索や社内システムへの登録といった実務が可能になります。 代表的なツールは以下のとおりです。 Web検索 社内文書の検索 メールやビジネスチャットの送信 表計算ソフトや会計システムへの入力 プログラムの実行 どのツールを持たせるかが、そのAIエージェントにできることの範囲を決めます。導入時は 「何をさせたいか」から逆算してツールを選ぶ と、過不足のない構成にできます。 メモリ：経緯と知識を保持する記憶 メモリは、 作業の経緯や業務の知識をAIエージェントに保持させる仕組み です。 LLMは呼び出されるたびに過去のやり取りを忘れます。外部に記憶を持たせないと、同じ検索を繰り返したり、前の結果と矛盾したりします。 Wangらのサーベイ論文では、メモリを以下の2種類に整理しています。 短期メモリ：今回の作業の経緯で、LLMが一度に読み込める範囲に保持する 長期メモリ：過去の作業記録や知識で、外部のデータベースに保存し必要なときに検索する 出典： 『A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents』（arXiv） 長期メモリに社内マニュアルや過去の対応履歴を入れておくと、 自社のやり方に沿った判断 をさせやすくなります。 AIエージェントが動く流れは5ステップ AIエージェントは、目標を受け取ってから終了するまで、以下の5ステップで動きます。 目標を受け取って理解する タスクを分解して計画を立てる ツールを選んで実行する 結果を確かめて次の行動を決める 完了条件を満たしたら終了する ステップ3と4を何周も繰り返す点こそ、AIエージェントが自律的に見える理由です。 目標を受け取って理解する 最初のステップでは、AIエージェントが 人から渡された目標と指示を読み取ります 。 目標が曖昧なまま動き出すと、途中の判断がすべてずれるためです。Anthropicも、エージェントは人の指示や対話でタスクを明確にしてから動き出すと説明しています。 出典： 『Building effective agents』（Anthropic） たとえば「競合の料金を調べて」という依頼だけでは、対象の企業や比較する項目が決まりません。AIエージェントによっては、不足している条件を人に質問してから作業を始めます。 依頼する側が 目標・対象・期限・成果物の形 を最初に伝えておくと、やり直しの少ない動きを引き出せます。 タスクを分解して計画を立てる 次に、AIエージェントは目標を 実行できる単位の小さなタスクに分解 し、取り組む順番を決めます。 「比較表を作る」という目標は、1回の操作では完了できないためです。Wangらの論文でも、計画は複雑なタスクを小さなタスクに分ける役割と位置づけられています。 料金比較の場合は、以下の4つのタスクに分けます。 各社の料金ページを探す プランと金額を抜き出す 表にまとめる 関係者に共有する 計画は最初に決めて終わりではなく、作業の結果に応じて組み直されます。計画の段階を知っておくと、 AIエージェントの作業記録から意図を追いやすく なります。 ツールを選んで実行する 計画が決まると、AIエージェントは タスクに合ったツールを選び、必要な値を指定して実行 します。 LLMは「Web検索ツールを、検索語『A社 料金プラン』で使う」といった指示を出力します。実際にツールを動かすのは、AIエージェントの実行環境です。 OpenAIの開発者向け解説でも、モデルがツールの呼び出しを返し、アプリケーション側がコードを実行する流れが示されています。 出典： 『Function calling』（OpenAI） 判断と実行が分かれているため、 実行環境側で「この操作は禁止」と制限をかけられます 。安全対策を考えるうえで重要な構造です。 結果を確かめて次の行動を決める ツールの実行結果は再びLLMに渡され、AIエージェントは 結果を見て次の行動を判断 します。 結果を確かめずに進むと、検索に失敗したまま空の表を作るといった誤りが起きます。Anthropicは、各ステップで実際の実行結果から進み具合を確かめることが重要だとしています。 料金ページが見つからなければ検索語を変えて再検索し、金額が税抜表示なら税込に換算するといった判断を、結果を見ながら行います。 このステップがあるため、AIエージェントは想定外の状況にも対応できます。 決まった手順しか実行できない従来の自動化ツール との大きな違いもこの点です。 完了条件を満たしたら終了する AIエージェントは、 指示で定めた完了条件を満たした時点でループを終えます 。 終了の基準がないと、AIエージェントは作業を続けたり、同じ処理を繰り返したりします。そのため、多くの開発基盤には処理回数の上限も用意されています。 OpenAIのAgents SDKでは、ツールを呼ばずに最終的な回答を出した時点でループが終わります。設定した最大回数（max_turns）を超えた場合も処理を止めます。 出典： 『Running agents』（OpenAI Agents SDK） 完了条件と回数の上限を両方決めておくと、 時間や費用が想定外に膨らむ事態 を防げます。 業務の具体例で見るAIエージェントの仕組み ここまでの5ステップを、 「競合3社の料金プランを調べ、比較表にしてSlackで共有する」 という業務に当てはめて確認します。通常の流れと、エラーが起きたときの動きの2つを見ていきましょう。 競合調査レポートを作るまでの思考と行動 この業務では、AIエージェントが 「考える→行動する→結果を確かめる」を何周も繰り返して 完了させます。 1回の検索や書き込みでは終わらず、結果を見ながら次の作業を決める必要があるためです。各周の動きは以下のとおりです。 周 考えたこと 行動 結果 1 まずA社の料金ページを探す 「A社 料金プラン」でWeb検索する 料金ページのURLを取得 2 ページからプランと金額を抜き出す 料金ページを読み込む プラン名と月額を取得 3 B社とC社も同じ手順で調べる 検索と読み込みを繰り返す 3社分の料金がそろう 4 比較しやすい表にまとめる 表計算ソフトに書き込む 比較表が完成 5 完了条件の「共有」を満たす Slackに投稿する 投稿を確認して終了 人が行ったのは最初の依頼だけで、ツールの選択や作業の順番はAIエージェントが判断しています。 自社の業務も同じように「周」に分けて書き出すと、 AIエージェントに任せられる範囲 を具体的に見積もれます。 途中でエラーが起きたときの立て直し方 作業中に想定外の結果が返ってきても、AIエージェントは 結果を読み取って別の手段を試します 。 毎回結果を確認しているため、失敗も次の判断材料として扱えるからです。B社の料金ページに金額が載っていなかった場合、AIエージェントは以下のように動きます。 プレスリリースや製品資料で金額を再検索する それでも見つからなければ、表に「非公開」と記載する 報告時に「B社は金額非公開のため要確認」と人に伝える ただし、立て直しの判断が常に正しいとは限りません。古い情報源の金額を採用するおそれもあるため、重要な数字は人が最終確認する運用が欠かせません。 「失敗したら人に報告する」と指示に書いておくと、 AIエージェントが無理に作業を進めるリスク を減らせます。 AIエージェントと生成AIの違いは仕組みにある AIエージェントと生成AI・チャットボットの違いは、 結果を見て行動を続けるループを持つかどうか です。3つの仕組みは以下のように異なります。 生成AIは1回の応答で処理が終わる チャットボットは決められたシナリオで応答する AIエージェントは結果を見て行動を続ける 違いを仕組みで理解しておくと、業務ごとにどれを使うべきかを判断しやすくなります。 生成AIは1回の応答で処理が終わる 生成AIは、 指示に対して1回応答を返した時点で処理が終わります 。 生成AIの中核であるLLMは、入力された文章に対して出力を返す仕組みで、自分から次の行動を起こしません。結果の確認や次の指示は、すべて人が担います。 たとえばChatGPTに「取引先へのお礼メールを書いて」と頼めば文面は返ってきます。しかし、送信や返信の確認は人が行う必要があります。 生成AIは「考える」部分を担う部品であり、AIエージェントは 生成AIにツールとループを加えた仕組み と捉えると、両者の関係を整理できます。 チャットボットは決められたシナリオで応答する 従来型のチャットボットは、 あらかじめ設計されたシナリオに沿って応答 します。 質問と回答の組み合わせや分岐を人が事前に作っているためです。想定外の質問には「担

items.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
items.description: arXiv:2610.27548v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

items.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
items.description: arXiv:2610.27888v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.

items.title: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.description: arXiv:2610.26950v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

items.title: Theorem prover Arend
items.description: arXiv:2610.27264v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-L\"of Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.

items.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.27746v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, sharp-421m-mlx achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 on one-shot consumer financial-choice tasks derived from held-out survey responses. Its accuracy exceeds GLM-5.3-Flash, Jev 1.13, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-6-Luna and GPT-6-Astra in the common benchmark (full test for the first four; matched 500-group sample for Astra). We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age-income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A response-stratified 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

items.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.28356v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.

items.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
items.description: arXiv:2610.16975v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

items.title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
items.description: arXiv:2610.25043v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

items.title: Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
items.description: arXiv:2602.04943v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to $\{0,\pi\}$, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.

items.title: WeGR: Towards Unified Generative Retrieval via Behavior-aware Tokenization and Preference Alignment
items.description: arXiv:2610.16979v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, effectively leveraging user behaviors in industrial GR remains challenging: existing SID tokenization methods struggle to preserve collaborative signals while maintaining balanced codebook utilization, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) for prioritizing high-value candidates suffers from sparse rewards when generated SIDs fail to match positive items. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified GR framework with two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) injects query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals into continuous representations before quantization, preserving behavioral information without disrupting codebook optimization. It further couples first-layer codebook refresh to reactivate underutilized codewords with fidelity anti-collapse regularization, which broadens gradient coverage over relevant codewords and penalizes collisions in deeper layers to yield behavior-aware SIDs with balanced utilization. For preference alignment, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons to alleviate reward sparsity, enabling coarse-to-fine preference learning from SID prefixes to complete items without auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments validate that WeGR improves retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a six-week online A/B test on a large-scale e-commerce search platform achieves relative gains of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in CTR, and 1.381% in CVR, while reducing CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%. These results highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of WeGR in industrial deployment, supporting multiple search scenarios and tens of millions of daily page views.

items.title: First Passage Attention
items.description: arXiv:2610.22714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.

items.title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
items.description: arXiv:2610.28673v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the 305M-parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (bit-identical to that of Gemma 4 E2B except for the final audio-embedding projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its pretrained weights; the adapters of our adapted system are additive and kept separate. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M-parameter CTC reader over a learned mix of four intermediate encoder layers and the encoder output; an adapted system adds 3.1M low-rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M-parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub-word language model. Against Cohere Transcribe Arabic (2.07B parameters), re-run on identical audio, the frozen system trails in word error rate (WER) but is not significantly different in character error rate (CER) on five of six human-labelled conditions, while running 3.4 times faster on CPU with greedy decoding. The adapted system is not significantly different in WER on a public Saudi customer-service call (19.20% against 19.27%) and on clean Emirati speech, is significantly better on telephone-coded Emirati speech, has a significantly lower CER on all six conditions of these sets, and beats a 0.6B recogniser fine-tuned on SADA in WER on all six; it still trails Cohere in WER on long-form Saudi speech. On a blind, human-corrected public call-centre sample it ranks 4 of 15 systems, behind three commercial APIs (significantly only one) and ahead of the other self-hostable systems by point estimate. An optimised joint decoder runs it at 139 times real time on one GPU. We also find, on our data, that references made by correcting machine drafts favour the drafting system. Code and public-set results are released.

items.title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.28767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

items.title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining
items.description: arXiv:2610.28838v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

items.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
items.description: arXiv:2610.28886v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

items.title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.29052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.

items.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
items.description: arXiv:2610.29073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.

items.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.29136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.

items.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
items.description: arXiv:2610.29162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

items.title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
items.description: arXiv:2610.29171v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

items.title: LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.29188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tables in real-world documents, including scientific papers, financial reports, and statistical summaries, frequently use merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Yet the lightweight formats LLMs handle best (Markdown, CSV) cannot express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) impose excessive token cost and parsing complexity. To enable systematic analysis of this trade-off, we introduce a taxonomy decomposing table structure into six atomic features (F1-F6) and corresponding complexity levels (L1-L6), and construct STB (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels. Using this framework, we propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a formally specified, minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and hierarchical headers. Experiments across five state-of-the-art LLMs show that LTEM achieves accuracy comparable to HTML, offers a favorable accuracy-token trade-off relative to HTML and LaTeX, and produces substantially fewer invalid responses than LaTeX; for table generation, LTEM is comparable to MultiMarkdown though HTML is best. We release our taxonomy, benchmark, and format specification to support future research on LLM-table interaction.

items.title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
items.description: arXiv:2610.29225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

items.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.29249v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse.
